title: The teaching office (CCC 85–87)
hookLine: the pope and bishops serve the word of God, not above it

lines: TWO THOUSAND YEARS OF PASSING IT ON.
cards: Play a game of telephone with twenty people and see what comes out the other end. A sentence about a purple cat turns into something about a pirate's hat. Every person meant well.
It drifted anyway. Now try passing on a message for two thousand years, through language after language. Catholics believe God didn't leave that to chance.
So who gets to say what it means? And what keeps them honest? Today: the teaching office.

teach.b: First, the name. Magisterium comes from the Latin magister, teacher. It's the Church's teaching office: the bishops, together with the pope, the bishop of Rome.

Catholics believe Christ gave the apostles the task of teaching, and that it passed to their successors. In Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells the disciples he sends out: "He that heareth you, heareth me."
Second, the surprise. Some people expect the Catechism to put the teaching office above the Bible. It says the opposite.

teach.h: NOT ABOVE THE WORD, BUT ITS SERVANT.
teach.b: Paragraph 86, borrowing from the Second Vatican Council, says the Magisterium is not above the word of God, but is its servant. It teaches only what has been handed on.
It listens to the word devotedly, guards it, and explains it faithfully. The pope and bishops are meant to be servants of the word, not its owners. Third, the old title.

teach.h: SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD.
teach.b: Since at least the time of Pope Gregory the Great, about the year 600, popes have signed documents with the title servant of the servants of God. It's still used today. Fourth, what it isn't.
A common myth says Catholics believe the pope can't be wrong about anything. Not so.

teach.h: HE THAT HEARETH YOU, HEARETH ME.
teach.b: The Church teaches that the pope is protected from error only under strict conditions, when he solemnly defines a matter of faith or morals for the whole Church. That's been used very rarely.
Most of the time, the teaching office does what the word says: it teaches, and it serves, so the faith doesn't drift in the telephone game of history.

how: Catholics pray for the pope and their local bishop by name in every Mass, in the Eucharistic Prayer.

the Church's teaching office, serving God's word

games.q: you're a bishop, and a new idea sounds exciting but doesn't fit what's been handed down from the apostles. what's your job?
o: teach it anyway; you're in charge
serve the word: teach only what has been handed on
games.why: the Catechism says the teaching office teaches only what has been handed on, listening to it, guarding it and explaining it faithfully.

practice: Bring to mind the pope, and the bishop where you live, if you know his name. Whatever you think of them, picture them as tired human beings with a heavy job: to serve a word bigger than themselves.
If you pray, you can pray that they listen well and serve faithfully; if you don't, you can simply wish them wisdom.

wordCard.voice: Magisterium. From the Latin for teacher: the Church's teaching office, the pope and bishops, serving the word of God rather than standing above it. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: servant of the servants of God, a papal title since Gregory the Great.

carryVoice: Your line: servants of the word. The week's lines: a monk remembered, become who you are, four pillars, made for more, two wings, handed on. That's another week.
